```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
options(warn = 1)
```

A lit surface shows its shape through brightness: faces turned toward the
light are brighter than faces turned away. When the fill also carries data,
the two compete for the same channel. This article goes through the ways
ggplot3d lets shading and colour share a figure: colour modes that keep
the fill readable, guides that show what the light does to each colour,
illustrative surface styles, line drawings, and lighting compared across
panels.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot3d)
library(ggplot2)
d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 36), y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 36))
d$z <- with(d, exp(-(x^2 + y^2)) + 0.5 * exp(-((x - 1)^2 + (y + 1)^2) * 2))
hill <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(shading = "smooth", colour = NA)
```

## Colour that survives shading

By default the light multiplies the fill: a face at a grazing angle is a
darker version of its colour, and a dark yellow no longer looks like the
yellow in the legend. `lights_3d(mode = "lightness")` moves only the OKLab
lightness of the fill and keeps its hue, so the colour stays recognisable
against its key. A face at the `neutral` angle to the light keeps its
colour exactly.

```{r lightness}
hill + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral",
    guide = guide_colourbar_3d(along = NULL, shading.range = TRUE)) +
  coord_3d(light = lights_3d(light_directional(), mode = "lightness"))
```

The colourbar now shows each value from shadow (left) to full light
(right), sampled from the same shading kernel as the faces. A palette that
changes lightness with value, such as viridis, loses the most under
shading, since shading changes lightness too; a diverging or isoluminant
palette leaves lightness free for the shape.

`"tone"` moves the colour toward a shadow and a highlight colour instead,
and `"overlay"` and `"soft"` are the blend modes of matplotlib's
`LightSource`.

```{r tone}
hill + scale_fill_viridis_b(guide = guide_coloursteps_3d()) +
  coord_3d(light = lights_3d(light_directional(), mode = "tone",
    shadow = "#22305a", highlight = "#fff3d0"))
```

## Illustrative styles

`material_3d(style = )` changes how a face responds to the light. Toon
shading quantises the response into bands, Gooch shading (Gooch et al.
1998) turns brightness into a cool-to-warm hue shift that keeps dark
regions readable, and normal colouring encodes the orientation of each face
as a colour.

```{r styles, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6}
plain <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  coord_3d(panes = character(), axes = character(), box = "none")
toon <- plain + geom_surface_3d(fill = "tomato", colour = NA,
  material = material_3d(style = "toon", bands = 4)) + ggtitle("toon")
gooch <- plain + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey60", colour = NA, shading = "smooth",
  material = material_3d(style = "gooch")) + ggtitle("gooch")
normals <- plain + geom_surface_3d(colour = NA, shading = "smooth",
  material = material_3d(style = "normals")) + ggtitle("normals")
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 3)))
for (i in 1:3) print(list(toon, gooch, normals)[[i]],
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = i))
```

## Line drawings

`hatch_3d()` draws the tone as hatching. The strokes are cut from the
surface by parallel planes, so they follow it in depth and are hidden by
nearer parts like any other line; darker faces keep more of them. With a
white fill, feature lines from `outline_3d()` and the plotter backend, which
draws strokes only, the figure is a line drawing that an SVG device writes
for a pen plotter.

```{r hatch}
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "white", colour = NA, hatch = hatch_3d(angle = 0, spacing = 0.01),
    outline = outline_3d(linewidth = 0.4)) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("plotter"), panes = character(), box = "none")
```
